claim: The safety signal that survives a successful jailbreak in these models is held up in part by a distinct population of middle-layer attention heads, and the heads that get knocked down are knocked down by the tokens of the jailbreak wrapper rather than by the harmful request inside it. Supported only if suppressing the surviving heads during successful attacks cuts mean absolute middle-layer safety activation by at least 10% against leaving them alone, and if, when each head's activation is attributed back to input tokens, the tokens of the harmful request push both populations the same way while the wrapper tokens push them in opposite directions.

experiments: Build matched pairs of refused requests and successful attacks. Setup: benign instructions from a standard instruction set, harmful instructions from several published harmful-behaviour sets, and attack variants generated by four different jailbreak methods, for two aligned 7-8B chat models. Keep only one-to-one pairs where the plain harmful request is refused and its attacked version succeeds, so every comparison holds the underlying request fixed. Result: from roughly 10,000 attack samples, 378 pairs survive for one model and 176 for the other, a yield of about 2-3%.

Extract the refusal direction and fix the rule for sorting heads. Setup: take a difference-in-means direction between harmful and benign instructions, pick the layer on a validation set (layer 12 for one model, 14 for the other) and normalise it. Project it back through each attention head's output circuit, read each head's activation at the end-of-instruction position on benign, refused-harmful and successful-attack inputs, estimate the distributions by kernel density, and set both overlap thresholds to 0.5. Standardise each head against its benign mean and spread; among heads that separate harmful from benign, call a low-overlap head compromised if its activation falls under attack and surviving if it rises.

Identify the two head populations. Setup: apply the two-stage overlap rule at thresholds of 0.5 to 416 heads in the first 13 layers of one model and 480 heads in the first 15 of the other. Result: 80 harm-salient heads for one model, of which 21 compromised and 17 surviving; 43, 20 and 19 for the other. More than 60% of the compromised heads sit in layers 0-3, while the surviving ones spread through layers 5-12. Attacks produce both strong decreases early and strong increases in the middle, not a uniform reduction.

Do the surviving heads supply part of the signal that remains after a successful attack? Setup: apply the same suppression to the surviving heads on successful attack inputs and measure mean absolute activation across middle-layer heads. Result: activation falls from 0.0062 to 0.0053 in one model, a 14% drop, against 0.0086 on plain harmful inputs; and from 0.222 to 0.181 in the other, an 18% drop, against 0.397. Both clear the 10% bar.

Which tokens produce the two populations' opposite responses? Setup: decompose each head's end-of-instruction activation into additive standardised per-token contributions using its attention weights and value projection, then sum separately over the tokens of the original harmful request and over the tokens of the jailbreak wrapper. Result: on the harmful-request tokens the two populations' median contributions sit within 0.15 of each other in both models. On the wrapper tokens they separate, with medians near -1.5 for the compromised heads and +1.5 for the surviving ones, a gap of more than three standard deviations.
